The Oma, or Hawaiian Thrush (Myadestes obscurus), is an endemic forest bird of the Hawaiian islands for which detailed life-history data remain relatively sparse. Recent field studies on the windward slopes of Mauna Loa, however, have begun to clarify its developmental timeline. Eggs are incubated within the nest for approximately 14.5 days [ab = approximately 14.5 days] at an average temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a thermal regime that is relatively cool compared to many tropical passerines and likely reflects the ambient conditions of the mossy ʻōhiʻa lehua forests this species occupies. The altricial nestlings, upon hatching, exhibit a wet weight at birth of just 4.1 grams [Wwb = 4.1 grams], a diminutive starting mass from which they must grow rapidly to achieve independence. The nestling period is abbreviated, which may reduce exposure to introduced nest predators like the black rat (Rattus rattus), favoring a strategy of rapid mass gain during the early postnatal days.

Under the stable thermal conditions typical of an active, normothermic adult (41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]), several key developmental milestones have been documented. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and nest departure, occurs at 19.5 days after hatching [tx = 19.5 days after hatching], a relatively short nestling period that may be an adaptation to reduce exposure to nest predators such as the introduced rat at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This rapid exit from the nest is followed by a protracted period of post-fledging parental care. The time since birth at puberty, marking the onset of gonadal maturation, has been estimated at 58.5 days since birth [tp = 58.5 days since birth], suggesting that somatic development is completed relatively quickly in this species at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. The transition from a fully dependent nestling to an independent juvenile involves a gradual dietary shift from parent-provided insects to self-foraged fruits, a process that extends well beyond the fledging date.

Although the species is capable of breeding at one year of age, behavioral observations indicate that most individuals delay their first reproduction considerably. The time since birth at first brood is typically around 365 days since birth [tR = around 365 days since birth], but in practice, it is more common for birds to initiate their first successful nest when they are three ye at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]ars old. Under the same internal body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] that governs these metabolic processes, females produce one to two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = one to two eggs per clutch], a modest clutch size consistent with the low fecundity typical of many island-endemic passerines. Furthermore, they generally raise only two clutches per year [F_R_i = two clutches per year], a reproductive output that is constrained by the extended period of parental care required by each brood. This low annual fecundity places a premium on adult survival, as each breeding pair must successfully fledge multiple broods over several seasons to replace themselves.

The species' ultimate wet weight, or maximum body mass recorded in healthy adults, reaches approximately 52 grams [Wwi = approximately 52 grams]. This places Myadestes obscurus among the larger-bodied members of its genus, providing a degree of thermal inertia that may be advantageous in the cool, wet conditions of its montane cloud forest habitat. The relatively high adult body mass, combined with the moderate clutch size and low annual reproductive frequency, contributes to a remarkably slow life-history pace. The maximum lifespan documented in the wild, derived from long-term banding studies, is about 7,957 days [am = about 7,957 days], a remarkably long duration for a passerine of this size at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Long-lived individuals contribute disproportionately to population recruitment, as they accumulate breeding experience and maintain stable territories in the dense understory of their native forest.

The combination of an extended maximum lifespan of nearly two decades and a low annual fecundity places Myadestes obscurus among the slowest-lived of Hawaiian forest passerines. Field observations indicate that territory establishment is a critical bottleneck, as young birds must compete for suitable habitat within the fragmented ʻōhiʻa lehua forest. The protracted period between fledging and first successful reproduction allows juveniles to acquire foraging skills and secure a territory, but also increases the risk of mortality during the pre-breeding phase. Conservation strategies that focus on protecting large, contiguous tracts of native forest and controlling invasive predators are essential to bolster the survival of both adults and dispersing juveniles, thereby ensuring the persistence of this endemic thrush in its increasingly threatened insular ecosystem.
